The installation shot I have is useless. It is a phone photo, taken against the window. Start with the size. Is it bigger than me?
Much bigger. It looms over you: about three meters across, hung low, so the bottom edge sits at your knee.
Good. Now the surface, before the subject. Is it matte, or does it catch the light?
It catches the light in bands. Standing in front of it, you see the varnish moving as you move. From the side the whole thing goes washed out.
And what is actually in it?

A figure standing at the far right, cropped at the shoulder. Everything else is empty floor, receding into a muted gray. The only warm thing is a lamp hovering at the top edge, tucked away where you nearly miss it.
What draws the eye first? Honestly.
The lamp, every time. Then the cropped shoulder. The figure arrives last, and I think that is the point: the painting keeps you looking before it lets you read it.
It is about three meters across, so it looms over you rather than sitting at eye level.

People assume my job is to say what a work looks like, and that is only the first minute of it. I write the verbal descriptions that visitors hear on headphones, and the rule I work with is that the sentence has to move the way the eye moves. So I start with the whole thing, how big it is against a body and what it is made of, and only then do I go in. Standing in front of a canvas, most people take in the light before they take in the subject, so that is the order I write in. The hardest part is not the vocabulary. It is resisting the urge to interpret. If I say a lonely figure, I have made the decision for the listener, and the description stops being a description. I say a figure standing alone at the far edge, and I let them decide whether that is loneliness.

I sell a lot of work to people who are looking at a photograph of it on a phone in another time zone, so describing a piece down the line is half of what I do. The mistake everybody makes is starting with the story. Nobody can hold a story about something they cannot picture yet. I start with scale, always. Is it bigger than you, or does it sit in your hand. Then the surface, because the surface is what a photograph destroys, whether it is matte or whether it catches the light and moves as you move. Then, and only then, what it is of. And I never use the word interesting. It tells the buyer nothing and it tells them I have run out of words. If you can make somebody see the corner of the room it is hanging in, they will believe the rest.

Welcome back. Today we are staying with a single photograph for the whole hour, which is either an act of generosity or an act of aggression, depending on your attention span. Our guest describes images for a living, and before we recorded she made me do the exercise myself. Look for sixty seconds, then say what is there without saying what it means. I failed almost immediately. Within about nine words I had called the sky ominous, and she stopped me, pointing out that ominous is a verdict and not a description. What struck me afterwards is how little practice most of us have at the plain half of looking. We are fluent in what a picture makes us feel and almost mute about what is actually in it. So that is the hour. The plain half, taken seriously, with somebody who has spent twenty years proving it is the harder one.
